variants.title: Decide the contract
variants.context: A URL shortener stores a mapping from a compact code to a destination and returns an HTTP redirect. Redirects vastly outnumber creations: the read path must be fast and available; the write path must keep code ownership unique and block harmful destinations.
variants.prompt: Should the redirect be a 301 or a 302?
options: 302, so links can be disabled or changed, with caching controlled explicitly by response headers.
optionFeedback: A permanent redirect can be cached indefinitely by clients, freezing the destination.
Speed differences are negligible; control matters.
The choice changes what you can later do with the link.
variants.hint: What happens if a browser caches the redirect forever?

variants.title: Decide the contract
variants.context: A URL shortener stores a mapping from a compact code to a destination and returns an HTTP redirect. Redirects vastly outnumber creations: the read path must be fast and available; the write path must keep code ownership unique and block harmful destinations.
variants.prompt: A link expires. What should the service return, and may the code be reused immediately?
options: 410 Gone, and the code is not immediately recycled.
optionFeedback: Recycling codes quickly lets old references point at new destinations.
404 hides the intent; immediate reuse is unsafe.
Silent redirection misleads users.
variants.hint: What could a cached or shared old link do if the code were reused?
variants.explanation: Do not promise that deleted codes can be immediately reused.

variants.title: Decide the contract
variants.context: A URL shortener stores a mapping from a compact code to a destination and returns an HTTP redirect. Redirects vastly outnumber creations: the read path must be fast and available; the write path must keep code ownership unique and block harmful destinations.
variants.prompt: Which invariant is the hardest to protect?
options: At most one active mapping for a short code.
optionFeedback: Code ownership is the correctness invariant; keep it separate from the high-volume read path.
Analytics may be delayed and lossy.
Latency is a target, not an invariant.
variants.hint: Which promise, if broken, sends users to the wrong place?
variants.explanation: Keep code ownership and redirect lookup as separate concerns.

variants.title: Size the read path
variants.context: The target is 100 million creations and 10 billion redirects per day with a 3× peak factor. Peak redirects are about 350K per second; at a 90% cache hit rate about 35K reads per second reach the mapping store.
variants.prompt: Peak redirects are 350,000 per second and the cache hit rate is 90%. How many reads per second reach the mapping store?
variants.hint: Multiply peak by the miss rate.
variants.explanation: 350,000 × 0.10 = 35,000 reads per second. The store must still survive lower hit rates during cache loss.

variants.title: Size the read path
variants.context: The target is 100 million creations and 10 billion redirects per day with a 3× peak factor. Peak redirects are about 350K per second; at a 90% cache hit rate about 35K reads per second reach the mapping store.
variants.prompt: The cache degrades to a 70% hit rate at the same 350,000 peak. How many reads per second reach the store?
variants.explanation: 350,000 × 0.30 = 105,000 reads per second, three times the healthy load.

variants.title: Size the read path
variants.context: The target is 100 million creations and 10 billion redirects per day with a 3× peak factor. Peak redirects are about 350K per second; at a 90% cache hit rate about 35K reads per second reach the mapping store.
variants.prompt: 100 million creations per day at 500 bytes each. How many GB of raw mapping data per day?
variants.explanation: 100,000,000 × 500 bytes = 50 GB per day, about 18.25 TB per year before indexes and replication.

mistakes.feedback: One hundred million times 500 bytes is 50 billion bytes.

variants.title: Trace the redirect
variants.context: The redirect path: receive the code, look it up in the cache, on a miss read the mapping store, return a 302 with explicit cache headers, and emit the click event asynchronously. Redirect correctness never depends on the analytics pipeline.
variants.prompt: A user opens a short link. Put the read path in order.

items.text: Receive the short code and validate its shape.
Look up the code in the cache.
On a miss, read the mapping from the authoritative store and repopulate the cache.
Return a 302 with explicit cache headers.
Emit the click event asynchronously; never block the redirect on analytics.

variants.hint: Analytics come last and cannot fail the redirect.
variants.explanation: Cache hit, miss, storage fallback, and asynchronous click event must all be obvious in the design.

variants.title: Trace the redirect
variants.context: The redirect path: receive the code, look it up in the cache, on a miss read the mapping store, return a 302 with explicit cache headers, and emit the click event asynchronously. Redirect correctness never depends on the analytics pipeline.
variants.prompt: The analytics pipeline is down. Put the read path in order and note what still works.

items.text: The click event is dropped or buffered; redirect correctness is unaffected.

variants.hint: Redirect correctness must never depend on the analytics pipeline accepting an event.
variants.explanation: Analytics may lose events by contract.

variants.title: Trace the redirect
variants.context: The redirect path: receive the code, look it up in the cache, on a miss read the mapping store, return a 302 with explicit cache headers, and emit the click event asynchronously. Redirect correctness never depends on the analytics pipeline.
variants.prompt: The cache cluster restarts cold. Put the path in order.

items.text: The store serves the read under admission limits and the cache is refilled.

variants.hint: Cold cache means the store takes the full miss load.
variants.explanation: The database must survive lower hit rates during cache loss.

variants.title: Draw the consistency boundary
variants.context: Creation and custom-alias reservation are strongly consistent; analytics and most read replicas may be eventually consistent and may lose events. Expired links return 410 Gone and codes are not immediately recycled.
variants.prompt: Two users request the same custom alias at the same instant. Which consistency does reservation need?
options: Strong consistency; only one reservation may win.
optionFeedback: Alias reservation protects the ownership invariant.
Eventual consistency would let both succeed.
Last-writer-wins breaks the invariant.
variants.explanation: Creation and custom-alias reservation are strongly consistent.

variants.title: Draw the consistency boundary
variants.context: Creation and custom-alias reservation are strongly consistent; analytics and most read replicas may be eventually consistent and may lose events. Expired links return 410 Gone and codes are not immediately recycled.
variants.prompt: A dashboard shows click counts a few minutes behind. Acceptable?
options: Yes. Analytics may be delayed and may occasionally lose events.
Only if delay is under one second.
optionFeedback: The contract deliberately excludes real-time strongly consistent analytics.
Exactness is not promised.
Seconds versus minutes is a product choice inside the contract.
variants.hint: What did the first-version boundary exclude?
variants.explanation: No strongly consistent real-time analytics dashboard.

variants.title: Draw the consistency boundary
variants.context: Creation and custom-alias reservation are strongly consistent; analytics and most read replicas may be eventually consistent and may lose events. Expired links return 410 Gone and codes are not immediately recycled.
variants.prompt: Read replicas serve redirects and one lags by two seconds after a link is disabled. What is true?
options: That is within the eventual-consistency contract for reads; disabling propagates shortly.
optionFeedback: Most read replicas may be eventually consistent.
Brief staleness after disable is a stated trade-off.
Strong reads everywhere would cost the read path its scale.

variants.title: Size the hot set
variants.context: Cache the frequently requested fraction, not all history. Instance count is peak load divided by tested capacity with headroom. Prevent enumeration of sequential IDs.
variants.prompt: Should the cache hold all 91 TB of historical mappings?
options: No. Cache the frequently requested fraction based on measured popularity.
optionFeedback: Popularity is skewed; the working set is far smaller.
91 TB of RAM is not a design.
Misses are normal and bounded by the store’s capacity.
variants.explanation: Measure popularity and object overhead before sizing.

variants.title: Size the hot set
variants.context: Cache the frequently requested fraction, not all history. Instance count is peak load divided by tested capacity with headroom. Prevent enumeration of sequential IDs.
variants.prompt: How should the number of redirect instances be decided?
options: Benchmark a representative handler, cache client, and query; instances = peak load ÷ tested capacity, with headroom.
Match the number of cache nodes.
optionFeedback: Do not invent server counts.
Guesses are not capacity plans.
Cache nodes and handlers scale on different signals.
variants.hint: What is the tested capacity of one instance?

variants.title: Size the hot set
variants.context: Cache the frequently requested fraction, not all history. Instance count is peak load divided by tested capacity with headroom. Prevent enumeration of sequential IDs.
variants.prompt: Codes are generated from a sequential counter. What is the risk?
options: Easy enumeration of every link; obscure the mapping from internal IDs.
optionFeedback: Sequential codes expose neighbours.
Enumeration is a stated guardrail.
Counters do not collide; they leak.
variants.hint: What can someone learn from code N+1?
variants.explanation: Prevent easy enumeration of sequential internal IDs.
